lessons.title: AVL rotations preserve ordering
lessons.learning_goal: Explain how a right rotation repairs a left-left imbalance while keeping the in-order key sequence unchanged.

approved_facts.statement: The balance factor of a node is the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree.
An AVL tree allows only balance factors of -1, 0, or 1 at every node.
Inserting 30, 20, 10 in that order creates a left chain in which node 30 has balance factor 2.
A right rotation at 30 makes 20 the root, with 10 as its left child and 30 as its right child.
A rotation changes only a constant number of links and preserves the in-order sequence of keys.

segments.spoken_text: Insert thirty, twenty, ten. Tree looks fine, right?
Hardly. Balance factor is left height minus right height. Thirty has left height two, right height zero: factor two. AVL permits only negative one, zero, one.
So I just delete ten and call the tree balanced!
Brilliant, destroy data. No. Rotate right at thirty: twenty becomes root, ten stays left, thirty drops to the right.
But rotating must scramble the sorted order, surely?
Surely not. Reading left, root, right still gives ten, twenty, thirty. Rotations change only a few links, keep order, and bring every factor back to zero.
Quick recall: what does a rotation preserve?

quizzes.prompt: After inserting 30, 20, 10 in that order into an AVL tree, which repair fixes the node holding 30?
options: Left rotation at 30
Right rotation at 30
Left rotation at 10, then right rotation at 30
No rotation is needed
quizzes.explanation: The chain leans left, so node 30 has balance factor 2 and a single right rotation at 30 makes 20 the root.

quizzes.prompt: Which property must an AVL rotation keep unchanged?
options: Each node's original parent
The number of leaf nodes
The in-order sequence of keys
The key stored at the root
quizzes.explanation: Rotations only relink a few nodes, so reading the tree left, root, right still yields the same sorted keys.

lessons.title: The left-right AVL case
lessons.learning_goal: Show why a left-right imbalance needs a left rotation at the child followed by a right rotation at the unbalanced node.

approved_facts.statement: Inserting 30, 10, 20 makes 10 the left child of 30 and 20 the right child of 10.
Node 30 then has balance factor 2, while its left child 10 has balance factor -1.
A single right rotation at 30 would make 10 the root with a right-heavy shape, so it does not fix the bend.
A left rotation at 10 raises 20 and turns the bend into a straight left chain 30, 20, 10.
A right rotation at 30 then makes 20 the root with 10 on the left and 30 on the right, preserving in-order 10, 20, 30.

segments.spoken_text: Insert thirty, ten, then twenty.
Ten becomes thirty's left child; twenty lands as ten's right child.
Thirty now has left height two and right height zero, so its balance factor is two.
But ten leans right: left height zero, right height one, factor negative one. A single right rotation at thirty would only tilt the tree the other way.
So rotate left at ten first. Twenty rises, ten becomes its left child, and the bend becomes a straight left chain.
Then rotate right at thirty. Twenty is root, ten is left, thirty is right, and every factor is zero.
Left-right case: which rotation comes first, and where?

quizzes.prompt: In the insertion order 30, 10, 20, what is the balance factor of the node holding 10 before any rotation?
quizzes.explanation: Node 10 has no left subtree and a right child 20, so left height 0 minus right height 1 gives -1.

quizzes.prompt: For a node whose left child is right-heavy, what is the first repair step?
options: Rotate right at the unbalanced node
Rotate left at the left child
Rotate left at the unbalanced node
Rotate right at the left child
quizzes.explanation: The left child must first be rotated left to straighten the bend; only then can a right rotation fix the unbalanced node.

lessons.title: Insert into a min-heap
lessons.learning_goal: Trace insertion of 1 into the min-heap array [2, 5, 4, 9] using append and sift-up with the zero-based parent formula.

approved_facts.statement: A heap is a complete binary tree, and in a min-heap each parent is less than or equal to its children.
In a zero-based array, the parent of index i is at floor((i-1)/2).
Insertion appends the new value at the next array position, then swaps it upward while it is smaller than its parent.
Sift-up performs at most as many swaps as the height of the tree.

segments.spoken_text: Insert one into this min-heap array.
The array is two, five, four, nine. Append one at index four, keeping the tree complete.
Index four's parent is floor of three halves, so index one, holding five.
Five is bigger than one, so they swap. The array becomes two, one, four, nine, five.
One now sits at index one; its parent, index zero, holds two. Two exceeds one, so swap again.
One reaches the root, giving one, two, four, nine, five. Only two swaps were needed. Every parent is now no larger than its children, and swaps never exceed tree height.
Cue: append last, compare with parent, swap while smaller.

quizzes.prompt: In a zero-based array heap, what is the parent index of the node at index 6?
quizzes.explanation: The formula floor((6-1)/2) equals floor(2.5), which is 2.

quizzes.prompt: Starting from the min-heap array [2, 5, 4, 9], what is the array after inserting 1 and restoring heap order?
quizzes.explanation: The 1 is appended at index 4, swaps with 5, then swaps with 2, ending at the root.

lessons.title: Extract the minimum correctly
lessons.learning_goal: Trace extract-min on [1, 2, 4, 9, 5] by moving the last item to the root and sifting down with the smaller child.

approved_facts.statement: In a min-heap the minimum value is stored at the root, array index 0.
Extract-min removes the root, moves the last array element to the root, and shrinks the array by one.
The children of index i are at indices 2i+1 and 2i+2 in a zero-based array.
Sift-down swaps the moved value with its smaller child while that child is smaller than the value.
Extracting the minimum from [1, 2, 4, 9, 5] produces [2, 5, 4, 9].

segments.spoken_text: Remove the smallest value: one.
In array one, two, four, nine, five, the minimum waits at the root.
Do not slide everything left. Move the last item, five, to the root, shrinking the array to five, two, four, nine.
Five is too big at the top. Its children are two and four; swap with the smaller child, two.
Array: two, five, four, nine. Now five has one child, nine. Five is smaller, so sifting stops.
Swapping five with four instead would leave four above two, breaking the heap rule. The smaller child must rise.
Cue: last item to root, then sink via the smaller child.

quizzes.prompt: During extract-min on [1, 2, 4, 9, 5], which value is moved to the root before sifting begins?
quizzes.explanation: The last array element, 5, replaces the removed root to keep the tree complete.

quizzes.prompt: When a moved value sinks in a min-heap, why does the choice of which child to swap with matter?
options: It guarantees the array becomes fully sorted
It shortens the tree by one level
It avoids ever moving the original last element
It keeps the new parent no larger than its other child
quizzes.explanation: Raising the smaller child ensures the new parent is at most the other child; raising the larger would break the heap rule.

lessons.title: Why bottom-up heap building is linear
lessons.learning_goal: Explain with a seven-node example why sifting down from the last parent costs O(n), while successive insertion costs O(n log n) in the worst case.

approved_facts.statement: Bottom-up heap construction runs sift-down on each non-leaf node from the last parent back to the root.
In a seven-node complete tree, four nodes are leaves, two nodes are one level above leaves, and one node is the root.
A sift-down can swap at most as many times as the node's height, so the seven-node example needs at most 2*1 + 1*2 = 4 swaps.
Building by successive insertion can need up to 4*2 + 2*1 = 10 swaps for the same seven nodes.
Bottom-up building is O(n) because about half the nodes are leaves and few nodes have large height, while successive insertion is O(n log n) in the worst case.

segments.spoken_text: Build a heap from seven unsorted values.
Bottom-up building starts at the last parent and sifts each node down, moving toward the root.
Among seven nodes, four leaves need no work. Two nodes one level above leaves can swap at most once each; the root at most twice.
That totals at most four swaps. Successive insertion may need ten: four bottom nodes climb twice, two middle nodes once.
Scaling up, about half the nodes are leaves, and tall sift-downs are rare, so total work is order n.
Repeated insertion has no such discount: its worst case is order n log n.
Cue: leaves are cheap, so bottom-up is linear.

quizzes.prompt: Why is bottom-up heap construction linear in the number of nodes?
options: It sorts the input before building
It only repairs the root node
Every node swaps exactly once
Most nodes are near the bottom and need little or no sift-down work
quizzes.explanation: About half the nodes are leaves needing no work, and each higher level has fewer nodes, so total sift-down cost sums to O(n).

quizzes.prompt: What is the tight worst-case time to build a heap of n keys by inserting them one at a time into an empty heap?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
quizzes.explanation: Many insertions can sift up about log n levels each, so the worst case totals O(n log n).

lessons.title: A heap is not a search tree
lessons.learning_goal: Distinguish the parent-to-child ordering of a min-heap from the left-versus-right ordering of a binary search tree.

approved_facts.statement: A min-heap requires each parent to be less than or equal to its children, giving the minimum at the root.
A heap places no required ordering between a left child and a right child.
A binary search tree requires keys in the left subtree to be smaller and keys in the right subtree to be larger than the node.
The array [1, 5, 2] is a valid min-heap, but its left child 5 is larger than the root 1, so it is not a binary search tree.
Comparing a target with a heap node does not tell you which child to follow, whereas a binary search tree comparison does.

segments.spoken_text: A min-heap is basically a search tree, right?
Oh, basically. Take array one, five, two. Root one, left child five, right child two. Perfectly valid heap.
Great, so smaller things go left, and I can search by comparing!
Wrong again. Five sits left of one, yet five is larger. Search trees need smaller keys left, larger keys right. Heaps only relate parents to children.
Fine, but to find two, I compare with one and go left?
No. Both children exceed one, so the root gives no direction. Heaps expose the minimum fast; search trees guide lookups.
Cue: heaps order parent-child; search trees order left versus right.

quizzes.prompt: Which array, read as a complete tree in level order, is a valid min-heap but not a binary search tree?
quizzes.explanation: In [1, 5, 2] every parent is at most its children, but the left child 5 is larger than the root, which a search tree forbids.

quizzes.prompt: Which statement is guaranteed for every min-heap?
options: The smallest key is at the root
Every left child is smaller than its right sibling
An in-order walk produces sorted keys
Searching any key follows a single root-to-leaf path
quizzes.explanation: The heap rule makes each parent no larger than its children, so the minimum must be at the root; nothing orders siblings or supports in-order sorting.

visual_plan.equation: not BST order: left subtree may be larger
not BST order: left subtree may be larger
not BST order: left subtree may be larger

lessons.title: Where cost of goods sold comes from
lessons.learning_goal: Compute periodic cost of goods sold as beginning inventory plus net purchases minus ending inventory.

approved_facts.statement: Under the periodic system, cost of goods sold equals beginning inventory plus net purchases minus ending inventory.
Beginning inventory plus net purchases is the cost of goods available for sale.
In a hypothetical example, beginning inventory of $1,000 plus net purchases of $4,000 gives $5,000 of goods available for sale.
Ending inventory of $1,200 is still unsold, so it remains an asset instead of becoming expense.
Cost of goods sold in the example is $5,000 minus $1,200, which equals $3,800.

segments.spoken_text: COGS is just everything we bought, right?
Brilliant. Purchases alone ignore inventory you already owned and inventory that remains unsold.
Fine. So we start with beginning inventory of one thousand dollars?
Yes. Add net purchases of four thousand, and five thousand dollars of goods were available for sale.
Then all five thousand becomes expense, because we owned it during the period?
Wrong again. Twelve hundred dollars is still unsold at period end, so subtract that ending inventory.
So five thousand minus twelve hundred leaves thirty-eight hundred as cost of goods sold?
Correct. Remember the formula: beginning plus purchases minus ending equals COGS.

quizzes.prompt: Under the periodic system, a firm has beginning inventory of $2,000, net purchases of $6,000, and ending inventory of $1,500. What is cost of goods sold?
quizzes.explanation: Goods available for sale are $2,000 + $6,000 = $8,000. Subtracting $1,500 of ending inventory leaves $6,500.

quizzes.prompt: Why is ending inventory subtracted when computing periodic cost of goods sold?
options: It is an expense that was already paid in cash
It represents purchases that were returned to suppliers
Those goods are still unsold, so their cost stays in inventory as an asset
It is the profit earned on goods that were sold
quizzes.explanation: Only the cost of goods actually sold becomes expense. Unsold goods remain an asset on the balance sheet.

lessons.title: A sale makes two journal entries
lessons.learning_goal: Record a perpetual-system cash sale with a revenue entry at selling price and a cost entry at inventory cost.

approved_facts.statement: A perpetual inventory system updates inventory records at the time of each sale and purchase.
In a hypothetical $100 cash sale, the revenue entry debits Cash $100 and credits Sales Revenue $100.
If the goods cost $60, the cost entry debits Cost of Goods Sold $60 and credits Inventory $60.
The $100 selling price minus the $60 cost leaves $40 of gross profit on that sale.
Each journal entry has equal debits and credits.

segments.spoken_text: One sale triggers two separate journal entries.
Under the perpetual system, inventory records update at the moment of every sale, not only at period end.
Take a hypothetical cash sale: customers pay one hundred dollars for goods that cost sixty.
Entry one records revenue: debit cash one hundred, credit sales revenue one hundred.
Entry two records expense: debit cost of goods sold sixty, credit inventory sixty.
Inventory falls by sixty, cash rises by one hundred, and the forty-dollar gap becomes gross profit.
Each entry has equal debits and credits, so the books stay balanced.
Quick recall: revenue entry at price, expense entry at cost.

quizzes.prompt: In a perpetual system, goods costing $80 are sold on account for $130. Which entry records the cost side of the sale?
options: Debit Cost of Goods Sold $80, credit Inventory $80
Debit Inventory $80, credit Cost of Goods Sold $80
Debit Cost of Goods Sold $130, credit Inventory $130
Debit Accounts Receivable $80, credit Sales Revenue $80
quizzes.explanation: The cost entry uses the inventory cost of $80: expense goes up with a debit and inventory goes down with a credit.

quizzes.prompt: A perpetual-system cash sale is made for $100 on goods that cost $60. How much gross profit does that sale produce?
quizzes.explanation: Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold, which is $100 - $60 = $40.

lessons.title: FIFO and ending inventory
lessons.learning_goal: Assign costs under FIFO to compute cost of goods sold and ending inventory.

approved_facts.statement: FIFO assumes the earliest purchased units are the first units sold.
In a hypothetical example, 2 units at $10 and 3 units at $12 give goods available for sale costing $56.
Selling 3 units under FIFO uses 2 units at $10 and 1 unit at $12, so cost of goods sold is $32.
The remaining 2 units cost $12 each, so ending inventory is $24.
Cost of goods sold plus ending inventory equals goods available for sale: $32 + $24 = $56.

segments.spoken_text: FIFO sells the oldest costs first.
A hypothetical store buys two units at ten dollars, then three units at twelve dollars.
That makes five units on the shelf, with total cost of fifty-six dollars.
Now the store sells three units. FIFO assigns the earliest purchased costs first.
Two units at ten dollars leave first, contributing twenty dollars. One unit at twelve contributes twelve more.
Cost of goods sold is therefore thirty-two dollars, the expense for this sale.
Two twelve-dollar units remain, so ending inventory is twenty-four dollars, and thirty-two plus twenty-four equals fifty-six.
Recall: oldest costs go to COGS; newest costs stay in inventory.

quizzes.prompt: Under FIFO, a firm holds 4 units bought at $5 each and then 2 units bought at $8 each. It sells 5 units. What is cost of goods sold?
quizzes.explanation: The sale uses 4 units at $5 ($20) and 1 unit at $8, for $28.

quizzes.prompt: A FIFO firm buys 3 units at $4 each, then 3 units at $6 each, and sells 4 units. What is the value of ending inventory?
quizzes.explanation: The sale uses 3 units at $4 and 1 unit at $6. The 2 remaining units cost $6 each, so ending inventory is $12.

lessons.title: Merchandise returns reverse both sides
lessons.learning_goal: Record a resalable sales return by reversing the revenue side and restoring inventory at original cost.

approved_facts.statement: A sales return of resalable goods reverses both the revenue side and the cost side of the original sale.
In a hypothetical $100 sale, the revenue side of the return debits Sales Returns $100 and credits Cash, or Accounts Receivable if the sale was unpaid.
If the goods cost $60, a perpetual-system return debits Inventory $60 and credits Cost of Goods Sold $60.
The inventory and cost of goods sold entry uses the original cost, not the selling price.
After the return, the sale's revenue and cost of goods sold are both removed and the goods are back in inventory.

segments.spoken_text: A returned item undoes both halves of a sale.
Picture a customer who bought goods for one hundred dollars; they cost the store sixty.
Today the customer brings the goods back, undamaged and fully resalable.
Revenue side: debit sales returns for one hundred, then credit cash, or accounts receivable if unpaid.
Cost side: the goods return to the shelf, so debit inventory sixty and credit cost of goods sold sixty.
Use the original sixty-dollar cost, not the selling price, because inventory is recorded at cost.
Net effect: the sale's revenue and expense both disappear, and the goods are back in inventory.
Recall: return reverses the price entry and the cost entry.

quizzes.prompt: In a perpetual system, goods that were sold for $250 and cost $150 are returned in resalable condition. What amount is debited to Inventory?
quizzes.explanation: Inventory is restored at the original cost of $150, not at the $250 selling price.

quizzes.prompt: A customer who paid cash returns resalable goods. Which account is credited on the revenue side of the return entry?
options: Inventory
Cost of Goods Sold
Sales Returns
Cash
quizzes.explanation: The store refunds cash, so Cash is credited while Sales Returns is debited.

lessons.title: Read a classified balance sheet
lessons.learning_goal: Read a classified balance sheet as a snapshot on one date and check that assets equal liabilities plus equity.

approved_facts.statement: A balance sheet reports financial position at a specific date, not performance over a period.

A classified balance sheet groups assets and liabilities into current and noncurrent categories; current items are generally expected to be used, converted, or settled within about a year or the operating cycle.
In a hypothetical example, current assets of $300 plus noncurrent equipment of $700 give total assets of $1,000.
In the example, current liabilities of $200 plus long-term liabilities of $300 total $500.
Equity in the example is total assets of $1,000 minus liabilities of $500, which equals $500.
Liabilities plus equity equal $1,000, matching total assets.

segments.spoken_text: A balance sheet is a dated snapshot.
It reports financial position on one specific date, not performance across a period.
Classified means grouped. Current assets include cash and inventory, generally used within a year or the operating cycle, if longer.
Suppose hypothetical current assets are three hundred, and equipment, a noncurrent asset, is seven hundred. Total assets: one thousand.
Liabilities split similarly: two hundred due soon, and three hundred long-term.
Equity is the remaining claim: one thousand minus five hundred of liabilities leaves five hundred.
Liabilities plus equity also total one thousand, matching assets.
Recall: a dated snapshot, with assets grouped, then liabilities and equity.

quizzes.prompt: On a hypothetical balance sheet, total assets are $900, current liabilities are $250, and long-term liabilities are $150. What is equity?
quizzes.explanation: Total liabilities are $250 + $150 = $400. Equity is $900 - $400 = $500.

quizzes.prompt: Which item would normally be classified as a noncurrent asset?
options: Cash in the bank
Inventory held for sale next month
Accounts receivable due in 30 days
A delivery truck used for several years
quizzes.explanation: A delivery truck is used over multiple years, so it is a noncurrent asset. Cash, near-term inventory, and short-term receivables are current.

lessons.title: Assets equal liabilities plus equity
lessons.learning_goal: Track how borrowing, owner investment, and a cash inventory purchase affect the accounting equation while it stays balanced.

approved_facts.statement: The accounting equation states that assets equal liabilities plus equity at a given date.
In a hypothetical example, the starting position is assets of $1,000, liabilities of $400, and equity of $600.
Borrowing $500 increases cash and liabilities by $500, so the equation becomes $1,500 = $900 + $600.
An owner investment of $200 increases cash and equity by $200, so the equation becomes $1,700 = $900 + $800.
Buying $300 of inventory with cash decreases cash by $300 and increases inventory by $300, leaving total assets unchanged.
Cash is not profit: borrowing raises cash without earning income.

segments.spoken_text: Assets always equal liabilities plus equity.
Start with hypothetical assets of one thousand, liabilities of four hundred, and equity of six hundred.
Borrow five hundred dollars: cash rises five hundred and liabilities rise five hundred. Now fifteen hundred equals nine hundred plus six hundred.
Cash increased, yet no profit was earned. Cash is not profit.
Next, the owner invests two hundred. Cash rises two hundred and equity rises two hundred, giving seventeen hundred equals nine hundred plus eight hundred.
Then buy three hundred of inventory with cash. Cash falls three hundred, inventory rises three hundred, and total assets stay seventeen hundred.
Recall: every transaction keeps both sides equal.

quizzes.prompt: A firm borrows $800 from a bank. What happens to the accounting equation?
options: Assets and equity both increase by $800
Assets and liabilities both increase by $800
Liabilities increase by $800 and equity decreases by $800
Only cash increases, with no other change
quizzes.explanation: Cash, an asset, rises by $800 and the loan is a new $800 liability, so both sides increase equally.

quizzes.prompt: A firm pays $300 cash to buy inventory. What is the effect on total assets?
options: Increase of $300
Decrease of $300
No change
Increase of $600
quizzes.explanation: Cash falls by $300 while inventory rises by $300, so the asset total stays the same.

visual_plan.equation: owner invests $200: cash and equity rise

lessons.title: Monsoon winds connected the Indian Ocean
lessons.learning_goal: Explain how seasonally reversing monsoon winds made scheduled round-trip sailing possible across the Indian Ocean.

approved_facts.statement: Indian Ocean monsoon winds reverse direction with the seasons.
Summer southwest monsoon winds favored sailing from East Africa and Arabia toward India.
Winter northeast monsoon winds favored sailing back toward Arabia and East Africa.
Predictable wind seasons supported scheduled trade among East Africa, Arabia, India, and farther Asia long before Europeans arrived.
The Indian Ocean network was not an uninterrupted, ideal peace.

segments.spoken_text: Winds once worked like a shipping schedule.
In the Indian Ocean, monsoon winds reverse with the seasons.
In summer, southwest winds push ships from East Africa and Arabia toward India.
In winter, northeast winds blow the opposite way, carrying ships home.
So a merchant could sail out with cargo, wait months for the wind to turn, and return on the same ocean.
Cargo such as cloth, spices, and ivory moved along these routes.
This predictable rhythm linked East Africa, Arabia, India, and farther Asia long before Europeans arrived. It was not perfect peace, though.
Recall: which seasonal change set the sailing schedule?

quizzes.prompt: How did seasonal wind reversal make Indian Ocean trade more predictable?
options: Winds favored one sailing direction in one season and the opposite direction later, allowing planned round trips
Winds blew in one direction all year, so ships never needed to return
Winds ended all rivalry and conflict between ports
Winds created new harbors along the coast
quizzes.explanation: Because the winds reversed on a seasonal pattern, merchants could sail out in one season and return in another. That regularity made scheduled trade practical.

quizzes.prompt: Which statement about the monsoon-era trade network is most accurate?
options: It began only after European ships entered the ocean
It linked regions long before Europeans arrived, though it was not an uninterrupted ideal peace
It was peaceful because no rulers or rivals competed
It connected only India and China, excluding Africa and Arabia
quizzes.explanation: The network joined East Africa, Arabia, India, and farther Asia well before European arrival. Describing it as constantly peaceful would be inaccurate.

lessons.title: Mali and trans-Saharan trade
lessons.learning_goal: Explain that Mali's wealth came from trade and taxation rather than creating gold, and that Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage displayed that wealth.

approved_facts.statement: Mali's wealth came from participation in and taxation of gold-related trade, not from creating gold.
Gold and salt were among the goods exchanged along trans-Saharan routes.
Merchants moving goods through Mali's territory were taxed.
Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324.
The pilgrimage displayed Mali's existing wealth and increased its fame abroad.

segments.spoken_text: Mali got rich by making gold, right?
Making gold? Alchemy remains unpopular among historians. Mali's wealth came from trade and taxes on gold moving north.
So caravans carried gold across the Sahara, and merchants paid nothing at all?
Nothing? Tax collectors would faint. Merchants paid taxes, and goods like salt and gold crossed trans-Saharan routes.
Then Mansa Musa's pilgrimage made Mali rich in 1324!
Wealth first, trip second. His 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca displayed Mali's riches and made it famous in Egypt and beyond.
So trade taxes built wealth, and the pilgrimage advertised it widely.
Correct. Recall: Mali profited from taxing what?

quizzes.prompt: According to this lesson, what was the main source of Mali's wealth?
options: Transforming other metals into gold
Participating in and taxing trade, including gold moving across the Sahara
Collecting gold only from European merchants
Printing money for Mediterranean markets
quizzes.explanation: Mali's wealth came from trade and taxation tied to gold-related commerce. Gold was not created by the state.

quizzes.prompt: What role did Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage play in Mali's reputation?
options: It created Mali's wealth from nothing
It ended trans-Saharan trade
It displayed existing wealth and increased Mali's fame abroad
It proved that Mali no longer needed merchants
quizzes.explanation: The pilgrimage showcased wealth Mali already had. It raised the empire's fame in places such as Egypt but did not create the wealth.

lessons.title: Mongol networks and exchange
lessons.learning_goal: Explain how Mongol political unification, post stations, and paiza supported some overland exchange despite devastating conquests.

approved_facts.statement: Thirteenth-century Mongol conquests were devastating, destroying some cities and killing many people.
Large-scale Mongol political unification in the thirteenth century reduced political fragmentation on some overland routes and facilitated some exchange.
Mongol rulers maintained relay post stations that supported messengers and officials.
A paiza was a passport-like tablet that marked authorized travelers entitled to support.
Not all of Eurasia was safe for everyone, and violence and danger remained.

segments.spoken_text: Conquest came first, connection second.
Mongol campaigns in the thirteenth century were devastating, destroying some cities and killing many people.
Afterward, large parts of Eurasia sat under related Mongol rulers, so fewer separate political borders interrupted some overland routes between East Asia and western Eurasia.
Picture a messenger crossing a long chain of post stations.
A paiza, a passport-like tablet, showed the traveler could receive supplies and fresh horses.
This did not make all Eurasia safe for everyone; war, banditry, and danger remained.
So exchange grew along some routes, even though violence had come first.
Recall: what two tools supported relay travel?

quizzes.prompt: Which pair of features helped officials and messengers travel along Mongol-ruled overland routes?
options: Relay post stations and paiza
Printing presses and monsoon schedules
Canal locks and tax ledgers
Walled harbors and movable type
quizzes.explanation: Post stations supplied relay support, and the paiza identified authorized travelers. Together they made official travel and communication easier.

quizzes.prompt: Which statement best balances conquest and exchange in the thirteenth-century Mongol world?
options: Conquests were harmless, so all travelers were safe
Conquests were devastating, but political unification helped some overland exchange
Exchange proves that no violence occurred
Exchange occurred only because all regions were independent
quizzes.explanation: Mongol conquests caused destruction, yet unification reduced political barriers on some routes. Both facts must be kept together.

lessons.title: The Black Death changed bargaining power
lessons.learning_goal: Explain how labor scarcity after the Black Death could increase worker bargaining power in some Western European regions, while outcomes varied.

approved_facts.statement: The Black Death spread across Afro-Eurasia in the mid-fourteenth century and caused massive mortality.
In some Western European regions, population loss left fewer workers available.
Labor scarcity could increase workers' bargaining power as landlords competed for laborers.
Authorities sometimes tried to limit wages.
Outcomes varied by region, and serfdom did not end instantly.

segments.spoken_text: A plague shrank the workforce.
In the mid-fourteenth century, the Black Death spread across Afro-Eurasia and killed huge numbers of people.
Picture one manor in a Western European region where many farm workers died.
The land still needed harvesting, but with far fewer workers, each worker became harder to replace.
So landlords competing for laborers sometimes had to offer higher wages or better terms to keep them.
Scarcer workers therefore gained bargaining power in some regions. Authorities sometimes tried to cap wages, and outcomes varied.
Serfdom did not vanish overnight; changes unfolded unevenly over time.
Recall: why did labor scarcity raise bargaining power?

quizzes.prompt: A manor has the same fields but far fewer workers after a major epidemic. What is the likely labor-market effect in some Western European regions?
options: Landlords gain unlimited control because labor is less needed
Workers may gain bargaining power because landlords compete for scarce labor
Wages must fall because there is less demand for crops
All obligations disappear immediately
quizzes.explanation: When labor becomes scarcer while work remains, landlords may compete for workers. That competition can improve workers' terms.

quizzes.prompt: Which conclusion about the aftermath of the Black Death is best supported?
options: Serfdom ended at once everywhere
No authority ever tried to restrict wages
Outcomes varied by region, and serfdom did not instantly end
The epidemic affected only Western Europe
quizzes.explanation: Responses and results differed across places, and some authorities tried to limit wages. The epidemic also spread across Afro-Eurasia, not just Western Europe.

lessons.title: Printing before and after Gutenberg
lessons.learning_goal: Distinguish woodblock printing, movable type, and Gutenberg's European press, and avoid the claim that Gutenberg invented printing.

approved_facts.statement: Woodblock printing existed in China before European movable-type printing.
Bi Sheng devised movable type in eleventh-century China.
Korean printers used metal movable type before Gutenberg's work in Europe.
Gutenberg's mid-fifteenth-century European printing combined movable metal type with a press and sped up book production in Europe.
Gutenberg did not invent printing; printing technologies developed in several places and stages.

segments.spoken_text: Printing did not begin with Gutenberg.
Earlier in China, woodblock printing carved an entire page into a single wooden block.
A block served one page, so changing the text meant carving another block.
In the eleventh century, Bi Sheng devised movable type: separate characters that could be rearranged for new pages.
Later, Korean printers used metal movable type before Gutenberg's work in Europe.
In the mid-fifteenth century, Gutenberg's European printing combined movable metal type with a press, speeding book production in Europe.
So Gutenberg mattered greatly in European printing, but he did not invent printing itself.
Recall: which method reused separate characters?

quizzes.prompt: A printer wants to reuse the same pieces to set a different page of text. Which technique fits?
options: Carving each full page into a new wooden block
Movable type
Copying the page by hand
Pressing a single unchanged block repeatedly
quizzes.explanation: Movable type uses separate reusable characters that can be rearranged for each page. A woodblock page is fixed once carved.

quizzes.prompt: Which statement about Gutenberg is most accurate?
options: He invented printing from nothing in Europe
He advanced mid-fifteenth-century European printing, but earlier printing technologies already existed
He introduced woodblock printing to China
He built the first metal type in Korea
quizzes.explanation: Gutenberg's press-based system was important in Europe, but woodblock printing, movable type, and Korean metal type came earlier elsewhere.

lessons.title: Why the Eastern Roman Empire lasted
lessons.learning_goal: Explain how the Eastern Roman Empire continued after 476, supported by Constantinople's location, defenses, administration, and Justinian-era law codification, while changing until 1453.

approved_facts.statement: The Eastern Roman Empire continued after the Western Roman Empire's end in 476.
Constantinople's location and fortifications helped its defense.
Imperial administration helped sustain government and tax collection.
In the sixth century, Justinian's reign saw Roman law collected and organized in a codification.
Constantinople fell in 1453, and the empire was not an unbroken, unchanged state.

segments.spoken_text: Rome fell in 476, so everything ended there.
Everything? Tragic news for the Eastern half, which kept going from Constantinople.
Fine, but it survived only because it never changed at all, right?
Never changed? Across nearly a thousand years? Adorable. Constantinople's setting and massive walls helped defense, while administrators kept taxes and government running.
So Justinian just copied old Roman laws into a pile?
Not a pile. In the sixth century, Justinian's scholars collected and organized Roman law into a lasting legal code.
So when Constantinople fell in 1453, the walls were useless?
Walls helped for centuries before 1453. Recall: name one survival factor.

quizzes.prompt: Which combination best helps explain the Eastern Roman Empire's long survival?
options: A coastal harbor that guaranteed no attack and no taxes
A defensible capital with strong fortifications and working administration
A complete lack of political or legal change
A permanent alliance that prevented all warfare
quizzes.explanation: Constantinople's location and walls supported defense, and administration helped sustain government. Neither guaranteed permanent safety.

quizzes.prompt: Which statement best describes the Eastern Roman Empire between 476 and 1453?
options: It vanished in 476 with no continuation
It continued, changed over time, and lost its capital in 1453
It remained unchanged until a Western emperor restored it
It was founded only after Justinian's legal work
quizzes.explanation: The Eastern empire continued after 476, including Justinian's sixth-century legal codification, but it was not unchanged. Its capital fell in 1453.

lessons.title: Matrix multiplication is row meets column
lessons.learning_goal: Compute a 2x2 matrix product entry by entry using row-by-column dot products, and see that order matters.

approved_facts.statement: The entry in row i, column j of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.
For A=[[1,2],[3,4]] and B=[[2,0],[1,2]], the top-left entry of AB is 1*2+2*1=4.
The top-right entry of AB is 1*0+2*2=4.
The bottom row of AB is 3*2+4*1=10 and 3*0+4*2=8, so AB=[[4,4],[10,8]].
BA=[[2,4],[7,10]] for the same matrices, so AB usually does not equal BA.

segments.spoken_text: Each entry is a row meeting a column.
Let A have rows one, two and three, four. Let B have rows two, zero and one, two.
For the top-left entry, pair A's first row with B's first column: one times two plus two times one equals four.
Top-right uses B's second column: one times zero plus two times two equals four.
Bottom row: three times two plus four times one is ten; three times zero plus four times two is eight.
So AB equals four, four, ten, eight.
Reversing the order gives two, four, seven, ten, so AB usually differs from BA.
Remember: row meets column, and order matters.

quizzes.prompt: In a product AB, which pair of vectors is combined to form the entry in row 2, column 1?
options: Column 2 of A with row 1 of B
Row 1 of A with column 2 of B
Row 2 of A with column 1 of B
Row 2 of B with column 1 of A
quizzes.explanation: Entry (i,j) of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, so row 2 of A pairs with column 1 of B.

quizzes.prompt: For A=[[1,2],[3,4]] and B=[[2,0],[1,2]], what is the top-right entry of AB?
quizzes.explanation: Row 1 of A is (1,2) and column 2 of B is (0,2), so the dot product is 1*0+2*2=4.

lessons.title: Rank counts independent directions
lessons.learning_goal: Explain rank as the number of independent directions and connect it to nullity through rank-nullity.

approved_facts.statement: The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent columns (equivalently, rows).
In [[1,2],[2,4]], the second row equals two times the first row.
In [[1,2],[2,4]], the second column equals two times the first column, so both columns lie on one line.
The matrix [[1,2],[2,4]] has rank 1.
Rank-nullity: rank plus nullity equals the number of columns.
For [[1,2],[2,4]] there are 2 columns and rank 1, so the nullity is 1.

segments.spoken_text: Rank counts independent directions.
Take the two-by-two matrix with rows one, two and two, four.
Its second row is exactly two times the first, so the rows add no new direction.
The columns agree: the second column is two times the first. Both columns lie on one line.
Every output lands on that single line through the origin, so the rank is one, not two.
Rank-nullity says rank plus nullity equals the number of columns.
Here two columns minus rank one leaves nullity one: exactly one direction gets erased to zero.
Recall: rank equals the number of independent directions the matrix keeps.

quizzes.prompt: A matrix with 2 columns has rank 1. By rank-nullity, what is its nullity?
quizzes.explanation: Rank plus nullity equals the number of columns, so nullity is 2 minus 1, which is 1.

quizzes.prompt: Why does the matrix [[1,2],[2,4]] have rank less than 2?
options: Its entries are all positive
It has more rows than columns
Its determinant is positive
Its second row is a multiple of its first
quizzes.explanation: Row 2 is twice row 1, so there is only one independent direction and the rank is 1.

lessons.title: Row reduction reveals the solution set
lessons.learning_goal: Use row reduction to find a free variable and parametric solution, and recognize an inconsistent row.

approved_facts.statement: Row reduction applies elementary row operations to an augmented matrix without changing its solution set.
For [[1,2,5],[2,4,10]], subtracting 2 times row 1 from row 2 gives [[1,2,5],[0,0,0]].
The remaining equation is x+2y=5; with free variable y=t, the solutions are x=5-2t, y=t.
A zero row means 0=0, a redundant equation that adds no constraint.
A row [0,0,1] in an augmented matrix means 0=1, so the system is inconsistent and has no solution.

segments.spoken_text: Row reduction reveals the solution set.
Start with augmented rows one, two, five and two, four, ten.
Subtract two times row one from row two, and the second row becomes zero, zero, zero.
A zero row is harmless: it says zero equals zero, a redundant equation.
Only x plus two y equals five remains. Variable y is free, so set y equal to t.
Then x equals five minus two t, giving infinitely many solutions along a line.
But a row zero, zero, one would mean zero equals one: no solution, inconsistent.
Recall: free variables give whole families; a zero-equals-one row gives none.

quizzes.prompt: An augmented matrix reduces to [[1,2,5],[0,0,0]] with y chosen as the free variable. Which describes the solutions?
options: Exactly one solution, x=5 and y=0
No solution
Only x=0 and y=0
x=5-2t and y=t for any t
quizzes.explanation: Only x+2y=5 remains, so with y=t we get x=5-2t, giving infinitely many solutions.

quizzes.prompt: After row reduction, an augmented matrix contains the row [0,0,1]. What does this tell you?
options: The system has infinitely many solutions
The system is inconsistent
A free variable exists in that row
The only solution is zero
quizzes.explanation: The row states 0=1, which is impossible, so the system has no solution.

lessons.title: Determinants measure signed area
lessons.learning_goal: Interpret a 2x2 determinant as the signed factor by which area scales, using a concrete parallelogram.

approved_facts.statement: The determinant of a 2x2 matrix is the signed factor by which the matrix scales area.
The matrix [[2,1],[0,3]] sends the unit square to the parallelogram spanned by its columns (2,0) and (1,3).
That parallelogram has base 2 and height 3, so its area is 6.
The determinant is 2*3-1*0=6.
A negative determinant means the transformation also flips orientation.
A determinant of zero means the transformation collapses area onto a line or a point.

segments.spoken_text: Determinants measure signed area scaling.
Take the matrix with rows two, one and zero, three.
Its columns are two, zero and one, three. They send the unit square to a parallelogram.
The base along the x-axis has length two, and the slanted side rises to height three.
Area is base times height, two times three, so the determinant is six.
Every region's area is multiplied by six. A negative determinant would also flip orientation.
If the determinant is zero, the square collapses onto a line or point, and area vanishes.
Recall: the determinant is the signed factor by which a matrix scales area.

quizzes.prompt: What is the determinant of the matrix [[2,1],[0,3]]?
quizzes.explanation: For a 2x2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] the determinant is ad-bc, which here is 2*3-1*0=6.

quizzes.prompt: If a 2x2 matrix has determinant zero, what happens to the unit square?
options: It collapses onto a line or a point
It doubles in area
It reflects but keeps its area
It only rotates
quizzes.explanation: A zero determinant means area is scaled by zero, so the square is flattened onto a line or point.

lessons.title: The null space is what a matrix erases
lessons.learning_goal: Describe the null space as all inputs sent to zero and find it for a concrete rank-1 matrix.

approved_facts.statement: The null space of a matrix A is the set of all vectors x with Ax=0.
The matrix [[1,2],[2,4]] has rank 1, so it maps the whole plane onto a single line.
Applying it to (-2,1): the first row gives -2+2=0.
The second row gives -4+4=0, so (-2,1) maps to the zero vector.
The null space of [[1,2],[2,4]] is the span of (-2,1).
Any scalar multiple of a null space vector is also sent to zero because matrix multiplication is linear.

segments.spoken_text: The null space is what a matrix erases.
Picture a machine eating vectors and squashing everything onto one line.
Our machine is the matrix with rows one, two and two, four.
Feed the machine the vector negative two, one, and watch what comes out.
First row: negative two plus two equals zero. Second row: negative four plus four equals zero.
The machine outputs the zero vector. Any multiple of that input is erased too.
So the null space is the span of negative two, one: a whole line of vanishing inputs.
Recall: the null space is every input the matrix sends to zero.

quizzes.prompt: Which vector is in the null space of the matrix [[1,2],[2,4]]?
quizzes.explanation: Multiplying gives (-2+2, -4+4)=(0,0), while the other choices produce nonzero outputs.

quizzes.prompt: What does a vector x in the null space of a matrix A satisfy?
options: Ax = x
Ax has length one
Ax = 0
x must be the zero vector
quizzes.explanation: By definition the null space consists of exactly the vectors that A sends to the zero vector.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors keep their direction
lessons.learning_goal: Distinguish eigenvectors from ordinary vectors using a diagonal matrix, including the effect of a negative eigenvalue.

approved_facts.statement: An eigenvector v of A is a nonzero vector with Av=λv, so A keeps v on the same line through the origin.
For the diagonal matrix with entries 2 and 3, the vector e1=(1,0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2.
For that matrix, e2=(0,1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3.
The vector (1,1) maps to (2,3), which points in a different direction, so it is not an eigenvector.
A negative eigenvalue reverses the vector across the origin, but the vector stays on the same line.

segments.spoken_text: Eigenvectors are special vectors that never move, right?
Never move? Brilliant. They keep their line, but may stretch.
So the diagonal matrix with entries two and three stretches everything by two?
Everything? Hardly. The first axis vector stretches by two; the second stretches by three.
But the slanted vector one, one must stretch evenly too, right?
Wrong. It becomes two, three, so its direction changes. It is not an eigenvector.
And a negative eigenvalue would send the vector off the line?
No. A negative eigenvalue flips it through the origin, yet it stays on its line. Recall: eigenvectors keep their line.

quizzes.prompt: For the diagonal matrix with entries 2 and 3, which vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3?
quizzes.explanation: The matrix sends (0,1) to (0,3), which is 3 times the original vector, so the eigenvalue is 3.

quizzes.prompt: An eigenvector has a negative eigenvalue. What does multiplying by the matrix do to it?
options: Rotates it off its line
Sends it to a perpendicular line
Reverses it along the same line
Leaves it unchanged
quizzes.explanation: Av equals a negative multiple of v, so the vector points the opposite way but remains on the same line through the origin.
